blocks.x: Because I formed a player at the Lyric Theater, a really good while, with John Roebichaud. That's why when he formed his band, I went with him.
That's where you went to play at the Lyric with John. Where did you go after the Brown Derby?

Well, after the Brown Derby, my next job, I think, was at the Cadillac with Rene. Rene had a job over there. Oh, yeah. Yeah, that's right. He got the job over at the Cadillac. Went for Old Man Coochie.
Yeah.
That's right across the street from the 5th precinct. What sort of place was the Cadillac Club? Well, that was a dance place. Rough, very rough.

Yeah, yeah. Very rough. How much would it cost to get in there? Do you remember? Pardon me? How much would it cost to get in? How much did you have to pay? Oh, I don't know. It was sort of a nightclub. No charges. Oh, no cover. You're just walking them by a beard. Yeah. Oh, yeah. I got you. Did the people want Dixieland in there? Yeah. Did they use their house with Dixieland?
All Dixieland, that's all they wanted. Dixieland building.
Mm-hmm.
Well, we stayed there until Papa Kutcher sold the place.
Who was in that band? Rene and yourself?

In that band at that time was Rene. Mm-hmm. Well, by the name of Jack was playing tenor from Chicago. I was on a drum. Mm-hmm. And that fellow by the name of a piano player by the name of Toots. Uh-huh. I don't know if you know him. I can't think of his last name. I don't know his last name.

Remember his name, Dick? Toots. Is that the real bright down? Yeah. Where does he live? Up in Shrewsbury? Somewhere around that way, yeah. Toots Washington. Oh, yeah. That was a fellow, Toots Washington. Yeah. Placed with Andy Anderson. Yeah. Oh, that fellow, Toots. Yeah. That was just a four-piece band there.
Yeah. And when Toots left, they had Walter D. Coo played piano with us. Mm-hmm. To the place closed.
Mm-hmm. Talking about Walter D. Coo, I believe you said you worked with him way back.
Oh, yeah. I worked with him pretty regular.
No, but way back you said you worked in a trio in the Depression?

Oh, I worked at Captain Petona, Fifth Wall Athletic Club. Yeah. Captain Petona used to own that. Mm-hmm. Who was that? And I worked with him over at West End Bungle for Old Man Albert Duboss. Yeah. And the band over there was Willie Paggio's on Trumpet. Mm-hmm. Old Man Sam Dutre, Sr. was on sax. Mm-hmm. Before then, they had Big Iron Lowry. You might have heard talk about him. Oh, yeah. Well, he was working there, and he got kind of sick, and he left. Mm-hmm. So Old Man Sam Dutre, Sr., he took his place, and Walter and myself. Mm-hmm.
Yeah. What year was that?
That was in the year of about 1930.

That was at the bungalow? Yeah. Yeah. So when would it be that you were playing at the athletic club? What year would that be? That was during the time of Depression. That was just before that? Depression, yeah. We would get no more than a dollar and a half a nine. That was what you were earning, a dollar and a half? Yeah. A dollar and a half a nine. What was the hours, how long you had to play for? Well, we used to go to work at nine and knock off at two. Oh, yeah, yeah. Nine to two. Who else do you say was in that trio? Charlie Love. Oh, yeah, Charlie Love. Yeah, Charlie Love. Could Charlie read music? Yeah. Charlie read music. Did you play all for music in that little trio? Yeah. And Walter Dink, who also read music. Yeah. But I mean, did they play anything like the blues or anything like that, didn't they?
Well, no, we didn't play that kind of music over there.
No.
With most of the orchestration.
Oh, yeah. Well, what was it then? A little dancing place they would have there?
Well, we saw it with a little night club, you know? Oh, yeah. Yeah, a little night club.

Yeah. How often would you work there? How many times a week? Every night. Every night, seven nights a week. Mm-hmm. Oh, yeah. Once we're on these early things, I think we'd have to do a little dance club. One of these early things, you told me that you played with Buddy Petit's band. Yeah. Well, you remember what, if you had a name for that band, what was it called, that band? The name of his band? It was Buddy Petit. It was all the name called. That's all they called it. Yeah. That was his name. How about Chris's band, talking about band names? Chris Keller's band, that's all. That's all they called him, Chris Keller's band. Not Chris Keller's. Why not his name? They didn't call it Chris Keller's jazz band or nothing like that, just Chris Keller's band. Oh, no.
Well, John Robichaud had his band name after him. But the Maple Leaf band, it was owned by old Kyle Gasper. But they used to call it the Maple Leaf Orchestra. That was an orchestra.
Yeah.
Sidney Desvins band was named behind Sidney Desvins. Was that an orchestra? It was an orchestra, yeah.
What's the difference between an orchestra and a band?

Well, to my estimation, the difference between an orchestra and a band. Mm-hm. The orchestra, they used the music. The jazz band, well, they just play anything, any, any, any. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah. And the number, by eight.

Yeah, that's it, yeah. Did you play a band? Yes. So, where did the word jazz come in? You remember that? When did they start using jazz, jazz bands? Jazz? Well, that was always jazz. They always called it that. Even those early bands, they would say they played jazz. The earlier bands? Yeah. They didn't call them dance bands. Well, yeah.

They had different type of music they was playing. You see, the real orchestra, they played jazz music, but I mean, they played, you understood what they was playing. Yeah. But the jazz band, they played, of course, they allowed to play things, song, and writing.

Yeah, yeah. So, so, if we took an ordinary straight musician from New York in a classical orchestra, say, and put him down in one of these orchestras, he'd be just as home playing as he would playing in his own classical orchestra.
That's right.
But how, if you put him in a jazz band, he couldn't figure it all out? Well, yeah.
Lots of them was pretty good. I mean, but they were, if you put an orchestration for them, they couldn't play the orchestration. No. But what they knew about it, they'd play that.
Yeah. Yeah.
See, lots of times you get a fella that's a musician, you get a fella that's not a musician. I mean, he's not playing like the part goes, but he's filling in right along.

Yeah, that's it, yeah. How did it affect you, though, when you were playing with the orchestras, reading drumming, and then you played with bands that didn't read, how did it affect you? You still play the same sort of way?
Well, no, I want the Lloyd Hall style of playing.
Mm-hmm.

So you definitely played different drums? I, I, I, I just figure, of course, in mostly, in mostly to my estimation, in mostly orchestration, you have to make the introduction, the first quarter, the first quarter and second quarter, that's all there's still now is left for you. Mm-hmm. Left for you to use your own judgment. Of course, if you have to play the drum music just like it's written on the paper, the band would sound like nothing.
Yeah. Yeah, I see.
In other words, you got to fill in.
I get what you did now, yeah, that's it.
And all you know when you play, you're playing. Yeah, I see. Yeah, I see. Yeah. Yeah, I see. Yeah. Yeah, I see. Yeah. Yeah, I see. Yeah. Yeah, I see. Yeah, I see. Yeah, I see. Yeah, I see.
Let's see, we're recording today at home of Alex Begaard. Let's see, this is 2724 St. Peter Street, and it's February the 7th, 1961. Can I have your name?
